If it is the Choice-affiliated entities or the Maryland injury-clinic chain, drop F01. The freight-audit engine and playbook are the only parts worth salvaging, and they should be tested in freight first.

objections: The 'sell retention first' fix is already a cheap, funded software category. CareKeep lists $199/mo (up to 50 caregivers) and $399/mo (up to 200), with automated day 1/7/30 check-ins, retention-risk scoring, referral tracking and a 90-day retention refund guarantee. QliqSOFT advertises automated 30/60/90-day new-hire check-ins plus real-time translation. Zingage raised a $12.5M seed (Bessemer, Oct 2025), runs onboarding and caregiver 'stay' surveys, claims 500+ agencies, and was added to HHAeXchange's Partner Connect network of 32,000+ providers in April 2026. The dossier's $500-900/mo concierge is 2.5-4.5x CareKeep's price. What is left is a human Creole/Spanish layer, and voice-AI vendors (Edesy, CallSphere) claim Haitian Creole and Spanish (vendor claims, untested).

'Unoccupied pricing' probably means rejected pricing, not an open gap. Four searches found no seller of pay-per-start or pay-on-retention aide recruiting. Every funded or established vendor chose flat monthly pricing with no guarantee: Carework ($720 to $1,865/mo, no guarantee text on its page), CareRecruit (per-location retainer, no refund, one agency per market), Boostpoint, Home Care Marketing. CareRecruit even pitches '$20-30K per year per retained caregiver' as the value, yet still will not underwrite retention. The vendors who know the funnel best decline the survival risk, and the founder would be the only one carrying it.

The $900 fee sits above everything agencies are shown paying. Staff referral bounties are $250-300 (HomeWell $300 after 90 days; ComForCare $250 after 250 hours). Ad-only cost per hire is about $104-188 (Boostpoint's own arithmetic). Flat vendors sell unlimited volume. My rough arithmetic from list prices: Boostpoint's $750 minimum ad budget plus Carework's $720 base tier is about $1,470/mo, or about $880 per hire at 20 hires a year and under $450 at 40. So per-hire pricing only wins for low-volume agencies, the ones least able to front $300 per start. The 'parity at 60% survival' argument also needs buyers to think in cost per retained hire, and one vendor claims 80% of agencies do not know their cost per hire (weak source).

Adverse selection and moral hazard. The agency controls most of what drives day-90 survival: wage, hours, scheduling, first-client match and supervision. HHAeXchange cites 84.4% turnover at $15-17.99/hr versus 53.0% at $18-19.99. Florida's minimum wage hit $15 on 30 Sep 2026, so many agencies sit in the bad band. The buyers who love a free-replacement guarantee are the weak operators whose aides churn anyway. Strong operators will not pay a premium for a guarantee they do not need. Verifying survival depends on payroll the agency controls, so an agency can terminate at day 85 to avoid the $600 and there is no way to detect it without payroll access. The dossier's own table puts gross margin at 6% (40% survival, $400 per start) to 20% (50% survival).

The supply shock hits the model's economics, not only the pitch. A May 2026 report ranks Florida last in home health aide availability. The Haitian TPS lapse touches an estimated 35,000 to 93,000 working Haitians, and sources conflict. One Miami report says two South Florida agencies closed after each lost 80+ authorized workers (single-outlet, unverified). A recruiter cannot create authorized workers. A flat-fee vendor passes rising acquisition cost to the agency, but this model pays it again for every free replacement. The founder's claimed edge, Creole community channels, draws on the group the dossier itself says is most afraid of outreach.

The customers are squeezed and the best ones build their own pipelines. Medicare home health was finalized at a net -1.3% for CY2026 (after a proposed -6.4%), including a temporary 3.0% base-rate cut to recoup overpayments. Florida's minimum wage rose to $15, and the Medicaid picture is unclear. Large operators run free aide training with placement (United HomeCare, Sunshine Health, Florida Memorial University) and hire in-house bilingual recruiters ($22-25/hr postings). That leaves small, thin-margin owner-operators as the buyers, who are the least likely to accept a $300 upfront fee plus 90-day billing. Medicare-certified skilled agencies, the likely MHC type, show about 34% aide turnover against about 79% for home-based care, so a family pilot would not represent the target buyer.

Any bigger player can copy the pricing in a quarter, and the data advantage is theirs. Indeed's Talent Scout AI recruiter launched in Sept 2025 (BrightSpring healthcare case study). Carefam raised $14.5M for AI hiring across care settings. EngineHire sells AI voice/SMS agents for recruiting, reference checks and candidate follow-up (BrightStar is an EngineHire customer). Care Hero lists Home Instead, BrightStar and Amada as customers. Zingage reaches agencies through HHAeXchange. Each already has the applicant and survival data to price an outcome tier, and the founder's only non-copyable asset is a paid Creole recruiter he cannot supervise linguistically. Content skills do not map to aides, who skew older than Gen Z (the finalist entry concedes this).

Even the success case is small and operations-heavy. The dossier sizes the tri-county pool at about $19M a year at $900. A 10% share is about $1.9M gross before missed targets, and $10M would need about 13,000 retained hires a year across several metros with a community recruiter in each language. At 10-15 hours a week that is a lifestyle service business with $300 and $600 invoices to small agencies. It is not a platform that compounds. The 'opted-in candidate base' upside depends on surviving the supply, margin and copy problems above. Willingness to pay is also unvalidated: no owner-forum evidence turned up in my searches or the dossier's, and the replacement-cost and 90-day-turnover figures behind the pitch ($2,600 per replacement; 25% to 80% early churn) are vendor claims with no traceable method.

SMALLEST TEST THAT COULD OVERTURN MY CASE: before building anything, take the exact term sheet ($300 at start, $600 at day 90, one free replacement) to 8-10 non-family Miami-Dade/Broward owners. If three or more sign without being steered by the grandfather's introduction, the pricing-gap thesis survives. objections: THE INSIDER-EDGE PREMISE IS LIKELY WRONG OR TINY. The F04 dossier dismissed mhcorp.com as 'a clinic group in other states', but that site fits the family firm closely. Legal name Maryland Healthcare Clinics LLC dba MHC Healthcare; founded 1987 by Dr. Semyon Friedman; his daughter Julia Peremel is named; it lists 130+ locations in DE, FL, MD, NC, VA and DC. That matches Asher's grandfather and mother. This is my inference, and one question to Asher confirms it. The site describes only specialty clinics (orthopedics, neurology, physiatry, PT, radiology, personal injury) and never mentions home health or home care. So the fork is: (a) MHC is a clinic chain, which means no aide hires, no family pilot and no 'MHC staff referral network', and a grandfather network that is Mid-Atlantic PT and personal-injury rather than Miami home-care owners. (b) The Florida 'MHC Area N, LLC' home-health entities (Boca Raton about 29 staff, Fort Lauderdale about 17, Venice about 35, per directories) are family-owned. No public source ties them to the family, and each has 17-35 staff, so a 10-20-start pilot is roughly a year of hiring at one small, probably skilled or Medicare-certified customer. The dossier itself calls that a weak proof of need. Either way, 'first dollar in 8 weeks from the family' is unsupported, and a family pilot proves nothing to peer owners.

THE IMMIGRATION-LAW SQUEEZE CANNOT BE FIXED BY 'NEVER ASK FOR DOCUMENTS'. Federal rules cover 'recruit for a fee ... on a retainer or contingency basis' (8 CFR 274a.1(e)). 'Knowing' includes constructive knowledge, such as having information that indicates a person is not authorized (274a.1(l)). The Supreme Court cleared the Haiti TPS termination effective July 27, 2026, and the D.C. court confirmed on Aug 5 that its stay is gone. Estimates put 93,000 to 113,000 Haitian TPS workers in Florida, with about one-third in home or long-term care. The pitch targets exactly the community that just lost status, and the network is paid at start, which rewards not looking. The other side of the squeeze: demanding specific documents is document abuse that DOJ IER has settled with staffing firms (Selective Personnel 2024, Key Fortune 2024). The only clean design, where the agency does I-9 and E-Verify and the network recruits no one from affected pools until the agency has verified them, removes the Creole-community advantage the whole pitch rests on. It also breaks the economics: day-90 survival now depends on immigration status, not engagement, and free replacements come from the same pool. E-Verify is mandatory only at 25 or more employees, so many small target agencies are not even covered.

LICENSING IS UNRESOLVED ON BOTH SIDES. A nurse registry is anyone who 'procures, offers, promises, or attempts to secure' contracts for aides paid as independent contractors (s. 400.462(25); AHCA license under s. 400.506). A health care services pool is a business 'providing temporary employment' (s. 400.980) and excludes nurse registries. Permanent W-2 recruiting is not squarely in either, but no source I found confirms that. Many small Florida non-medical agencies use 1099 caregivers (a CSI Caregiver Services posting recruits 1099 caregivers), and a fee for placing those looks like registry activity. Free-replacement guarantees and any bench feature drift toward pool territory. Level 2 screening is run by the employing agency through the AHCA Clearinghouse, so the network cannot honestly sell 'screened' aides. Agency clearance timing also controls the 'start' date that triggers the $300, which invites disputes. A $500-1,000 lawyer review will not settle a classification question that the statutes leave open.

THE CHECK-IN LINE CREATES DUTIES AND TAIL RISK A TEEN LLC CANNOT PRICE. Fla. Stat. 415.1034(1)(a) puts the reporting duty on 'any person' who knows or has reasonable cause to suspect abuse, neglect or exploitation of a vulnerable adult, with an immediate report to the hotline. Calls at days 3, 14, 30 and 60 with aides working inside clients' homes will surface such disclosures, creating reportable knowledge and discoverable records. I could not verify the non-reporting penalty. I found no Florida authority either way on negligent-referral liability for a recruiter. That means E&O and general liability cost and exposure are unknown, and one placed aide harming a client is the tail event for a two-person LLC.

HE CANNOT STAFF THE CORE DELIVERY, AND THE FEE STRUCTURE IS EASY TO GAME. He has no Creole, and the dossier concedes he needs a paid Creole-speaking community recruiter. That person owns the trust, the candidate relationships and the list. Hold-up risk is high, because they can go direct to agencies or another vendor, and an aide's phone contact is portable. The agency side has its own exits. Backdoor hires (rehiring the introduced aide directly) are the dominant dispute pattern in contingency recruiting. An owner can cut hours or terminate on day 85 to dodge the $600. Enforcing it means auditing owner-operators' payroll, with no leverage, and then small-claims suits over $600. Recruiters report fee suits taking months (one anecdote says 9 months).

THE CUSTOMER SIDE IS CROWDED, THIN AND UNDER STRESS. Five or more funded vendors already sell recruiting at $720-1,865/mo, CareerSource offers free help, and big non-profits run their own training-to-hire pipelines (all in the dossier). I also found no pay-per-hire competitor, but that is a pricing wrapper rather than a moat. Agencies are stressed: Southeast Home Care closed entities including Doral and Fort Lauderdale and laid off 178 in June 2026; CMS proposed a roughly 9% Medicare home health cut; and one undated report says two South Florida agencies shut after losing 80+ authorized workers. That raises non-payment risk on a day-90 fee. The Gen Z creator edge does not apply, because aides skew older (the dossier admits this).

TIME AND RUNWAY DO NOT FIT. This is a Miami tri-county field business (community recruiters, schools, owner meetings) run in 10-15 hours a week through college-application season, AP exams and finals. The day-90 fee means the first pilot cash lands roughly April-May 2027 if starts begin in January. The survival-curve 'data product' needs hundreds of starts, which is unreachable by summer. From his own profile, most of his applications are out of state (USC ED, Michigan, Purdue, UT, South Carolina, Penn State, Tulane; only UF and Miami are in Florida), so from August 2027 the business is remote or run by the hired recruiter. A pilot of 10-20 starts grosses about $6-12K ($300 per start plus about half surviving to the $600), before sourcing, the community recruiter, lawyer, insurance and checks. That is a poor return on about 100 hours, and it diverts him from the already-built freight-audit service, which is unsold only because outreach calls are pending.

PLATFORM RISK IS REAL BUT THE LEAST OF THE PROBLEMS. Meta treats employment ads as a special ad category with age, gender and zip targeting removed, enforced increasingly by automated detection, and repeated rejections hurt a new ad account's standing. WhatsApp requires opt-in, and it is piloting a monthly cap on messages to non-responders, so cold group outreach is out. That pushes volume back to churches, radio and word of mouth, which is trust-based relationship work he cannot do alone and the unsaturated 'community channel' pitch depends on.

result.title: Ground Truth Ledger (F02): post-critique verdict, dead as a company
result.one_liner: A buyer-side, blind, expert-graded accuracy test of AI back-office tools (OASIS pre-fill, advisor notetakers); the gap is real but the payer, the bench and the route to big are not.
result.pitch:
The strongest honest version of F02 is a buyer-side accuracy bake-off. An owner-operated home-health agency or independent advisory firm is about to pick or renew an AI tool that pre-fills OASIS items or writes meeting notes. Today it can check the vendor three ways: the vendor's own accuracy claim (95 to 98 percent, no stated method), a free checklist from QAPIplus or XYPN, or its own coders on a few old charts. Asher would sell a fourth: a blind test on 50 to 100 scripted encounters, graded against a gold standard built by credentialed clinicians and coders, with disagreements adjudicated and one plain number delivered to the buyer only. No vendor money, no badge, no publication.

The gap is real. Neither the dossier nor my search found an independent accuracy study of AI OASIS tools, and Asher has a proven edge in exactly this skill: his AI-text detector beat commercial detectors in his own blind tests, and his backtesting lab pre-registers strategies against a holdout.

It still fails, for reasons verified or confirmed this round. First, the MHC premise is almost certainly wrong. mhcorp.com describes Maryland Healthcare Clinics, a 130-plus clinic physical therapy and injury-care network founded in 1987 by Dr. Semyon Friedman, whose daughter Julia Peremel is named on the page. It never mentions home health, OASIS or AI. There is no family OASIS bench and no family home-health customer. Second, no payer has appeared: I found no agency that has commissioned a third-party test of an AI OASIS tool, and the existing budget line, human review at $40 to $70 a chart, belongs to sellers who bundle AI checking. Third, evals are a paid market only at the top. Vals AI says companies pay it to be tested, with labs, large banks and hospital systems as customers, and it just raised $40M; Mercor sells expert-built evals at scale. A vertical add-on from either erases a one-person entrant. Fourth, the only route to big is becoming the trusted standard, which needs years of vendor trust and legal capital, and a published score invites a demand letter that costs more than the whole budget.

Verdict: dead as a company. What survives is a method and a corrected map of the family's real asset, not a business.
result.why_now: Real but closing. The pull: GAO flagged few independent studies of AI coding accuracy (critic-cited, July 2026), CMS April 2026 Q&As keep coding responsibility with the clinician, and home-health AI funding is hot (Enzo $20M, Brellium about $17M, Apricot, Olli). The push against: URAC launched AI accreditation (first three accredited Aug 2026), Vals raised $40M in Aug 2026 to own neutral benchmarks, and Mercor sells expert evals. The window for a first-mover standard is closing, not opening, and it was never open to a one-person LLC.
result.customer_and_payer: Best candidate payer: the administrator or QA director of an owner-operated home-health agency, buying a pre-purchase bake-off out of the OASIS review and QA line (human review runs $40 to $70 a chart). Secondary: an RIA chief compliance officer vetting AI notetakers, and funded AI vendors wanting a score. No payer has been evidenced: two critics and my own search found no agency or vendor that has bought an independent accuracy test, and vendors want a badge, not an honest score. The family link is weaker than assumed: MHC appears to be a 130-plus clinic PT and injury network with no home-health arm shown anywhere, so there is no family agency to pilot with.
result.pricing: Only if someone insisted on running it: $5,000 list per buyer-side bake-off, because the first gold set costs $2k to $7k of expert time and $2,500 is at or below break-even; $3,000 design-partner price only when the buyer prepays and permits an anonymized case study; no vendor-paid badge and no published named scores; $1,500 a month re-test retainer only after a first bake-off lands. None of these prices has been validated by a buyer, and Mercor and Vals publish no comparable prices.
result.moat_path: None identified. The candidate moats are each copyable or conflicted: a credentialed expert bench (they can earn more at Mercor directly, and Mercor already holds 30,000 contractors), a private rotating holdout set (reuse contaminates it, so it is a recurring cost), and a reputation for independence (the brand Vals, URAC and KLAS already hold, and one an 18-year-old with family ties cannot claim). The only real asset is Asher's blind-testing method, which is a skill, not a moat.
first_30_days: Day 1 to 2: ask Asher's mother four questions and write the answers in one paragraph: Is MHC the Maryland Healthcare Clinics group (mhcorp.com)? Does MHC or any affiliate own a Medicare-certified home-health agency? Who runs billing, coding and medical records, and do they use any AI tool? Will the CFO give a 30-minute call? Output: MHC identity resolved yes or no, in writing.

Day 3 to 5: write the 10-call script and target list (below). One core question only: who did you last pay to check whether an AI tool was accurate, how much, and who signed? Zero decks, zero building. Output: a 10-row tracking sheet with columns for has-paid, budget line, signer, price named.

Day 6 to 14: complete 10 payer-existence calls at 2 to 3 per week, about 5 hours a week, the rest of the time left for school and freight-audit calls. Output: 10 filled rows and a count of how many name both a budget line and a signer.
